title: Colorado emissions for the swap: keep the donor's converters, O2s and …
ask: Should the LS keep its donor's whole emissions system - catalytic converters, O2 sensors, EVAP - so the car passes Colorado's test as a car of the engine's year?
why:
Larimer County is in Colorado's emissions program, and a 1982 car is tested every two years. Regulation 11 (5 CCR 1001-13) says that after an engine change, the limits and the emissions equipment checked follow "whichever is newest, the vehicle or the replacement engine", recorded on a vehicle evaluation form (DR2365). A 2005-2007 L33 makes the car a 2005-2007 car for the test: it must keep the donor's catalytic converters, oxygen sensors and evaporative system, and run clean enough to pass.

The answer sets DS03 (headers and exhaust: whether two catalytic converters and rear O2 bungs are designed in) and whether ls_devices LD11 and LD20 (the optional emissions parts) are wired. Collector plates waive the test for a 1976-1985 car only if it was registered as a collector's item before 2009-09-01 and never lapsed. It was read from the state legislature's emissions page; the 2025 amendments to Regulation 11 are not checked line by line. Confirm with Air Care Colorado before buying.
options:
(a) Keep the donor's whole emissions system: both catalytic converters in the new exhaust, every O2 sensor, the EVAP canister and purge, PCV. The ECU runs them. Costs the converters (about $200-600 for two direct-fit universal ones, confirm) plus the donor's own sensors and canister, pulled with the engine. Forecloses nothing, and the car registers.
(b) First find out the car's registration history. If it has held collector plates continuously since before 2009-09-01, there is no test, and (a) becomes a choice rather than a must. Costs a call to the county. Changes nothing until it is answered.
(c) Build without them. Cheaper and simpler, but the car fails the equipment check and cannot be registered in Larimer County.
recommend: (a), unless the county confirms collector plates held since before 2009 - then (b).
stops: DS03 (headers and exhaust), ls_devices LD11 and LD20, and the budget DS10.

title: Rear axle for the LS: a yard Explorer 8.8 on FB brackets, or a …
ask: Which rear axle carries the LS: a yard Explorer 8.8 on Drifting Dad's FB brackets, or their complete Ford 9?
why:
The stock FB rear axle is not expected to survive LS torque: broken diffs are reported on the stronger GSL-SE (option OP40). FB V8 builds found use a Ford 8.8 (an LS3/T56 FB on two shortened 8.8s with a fabricated Watts link; Drifting Dad's FB bracket kit) or a complete Ford 9.

The choice sets the driveshaft, the rear brakes (D-113 wants discs) and the wheel bolt pattern. An 8.8 brings 5x4.5 in (5x114.3) hubs, so the front changes to 5-lug too (Drifting Dad's kit with FC RX-7 hubs and brakes), and every wheel luxury chooses for C10 must be 5x114.3, not the FB's 4x110.
options:
(a) A 1995-2001 Explorer Ford 8.8 from a yard, which has rear discs and 31-spline axles, on Drifting Dad's weld-on FB brackets ($300) with their panhard bar ($220) or Watts bars ($300). The front goes 5-lug with their FC-hub kit ($300 plus FC hubs, bearings and brakes). About $1,000-2,000 all in (confirm the axle's price and whether it must be narrowed for the FB's track). Needs welding. Forecloses 4x110 wheels.
(b) Drifting Dad's complete Ford 9 for the FB, $3,500, 6+ months' lead time. Strongest and bolt-in, the most money and the longest wait. Also 5-lug.
(c) Keep the FB axle. Costs nothing now, but it is expected to break, keeps drum brakes, and is replaced later anyway.
recommend: (a), unless you want it bolt-in and can wait 6+ months - then (b).
stops: DS08 (rear axle and brakes), the driveshaft (DS07), the 5-lug front, luxury C10's wheels, and the budget DS10.

title: Accessory drive: compact ICT Billet, complete Holley, or a junkyard …
ask: Which front accessory drive should the LS run: ICT Billet's compact kit with A/C, Holley's complete 20-138, or a junkyard F-body/Corvette set with a 160 A alternator?
why: The LS needs a front accessory drive that clears the FB's frame rails, hood and crossmember. It carries an alternator of 160 A or more (D-457: about 163 A of load with every comfort load on), the water pump and the A/C compressor (the luxury A/C stays; the ECU owns its clutch, D-489). It needs no power-steering pump: the 1982 GS steers manually. Truck drives are too tall and wide. The FB V8 builds found used F-body accessories or ran a short Corvette-spaced drive.
options:
(a) ICT Billet's compact LS swap drive with A/C, Corvette balancer spacing, built for tight front clearance, with their 160 A ACDelco alternator option. Its price with A/C was not readable on 2026-10-16 (confirm). The steering pump is left off or replaced by an idler.
(b) Holley 20-138 complete drive (SD7 compressor, alternator, belt, tensioner), about $1,850-2,070. Complete and well documented, but a high mount, so the FB's hood line is the risk; the steering pump is deleted.
(c) A junkyard F-body or C5 Corvette drive with an aftermarket 160 A alternator fitted. About $200-600, the most fitting and fabrication, and the factory 105-110 A alternators fall short of D-457.
recommend: (a), unless its price with A/C comes in above Holley's - then (b), checked against the hood line at M01.
stops: DS01 (accessory drive), the alternator wiring (electrical Y83, LW29/LW40), and the budget DS10.
